title_original: Musk Review: Alex Gibney Offers a Probing, Terrifying Dive Into the World’s Richest Man
excerpt_original: A dense, probing, ultimately terrifying exploration of the world’s richest man, Alex Gibney’s four-hour opus Musk isn’t going to reveal anything new about the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX that you couldn’t glean from the myriad books, podcasts, and articles. There’s no smoking gun to…

blocks.text: A dense, probing, ultimately terrifying exploration of the world’s richest man, Alex Gibney’s four-hour opus Musk isn’t going to reveal anything new about the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX that you couldn’t glean from the myriad books, podcasts, and articles. There’s no smoking gun to explain his laser-like focus on domination or even his intense rightward political shift in recent years. Yet in sweeping across Musk’s life since about 1995—when he founded his first company, Zip2—Gibney nevertheless paints a damning picture in its totality and simplicity. That’s because for all his talk of AI, self-driving cars, and colonizing Mars, Elon Musk is a frighteningly simple person to decipher. The illusion of wealth, status, and brilliance that he carried through the 1990s finally gave way to actual wealth and status by hustling and grifting his way into a succession of companies that were already marginally successful.

You tell enough people that you’re an engineer, eventually they’ll start believing you. Thus Gibney is forced to confront two problems head-on. The first being that, as a psychological portrait, it’s not going to take four hours to explain Elon Musk. He may have immense wealth and power but, as Kara Swisher explains ad nauseum in the film, he’s essentially a child who doesn’t take kindly to being belittled. The second is that, as an ill-fated Twitter (or, as I suppose we have to call it now, X) exchange that begins the film explains, Musk was unwilling to talk to Gibney. Musk calls Gibney a “douche” and Gibney responds “douché,” effectively tanking any prospects of a sit-down.

For the first problem, Gibney wisely doesn’t try to complicate Musk. Instead the filmmaker has overwhelmed with anecdotes and evidence that prove a central thesis: Musk’s base impulses are to take credit for things he didn’t create and obfuscate when they go wrong. He’s a power-hungry oligarch and charlatan who is willing to pull every lever possible to achieve total control, if only to prove he’s the smartest guy in the room.

For the second, Gibney deploys a strange directional affectation that threatens to derail his purposeful critique. He creates a ghoulish AI Musk avatar—sitting in a gamer chair, dressed in a leather jacket, with a head that’s just a little too big—to “interview.” While all the words coming out of AI Musk are recordings from his countless interviews, it’s nevertheless a strange, distracting choice. It’s also one that the film returns to constantly, deployed as a rebuttal to the critics who Gibney trots out: former colleagues, romantic partners, and journalists, mainly. This choice is further compounded by the visual insistence on reimagining the world as a type of Matrix -like simulation where his acquisition of wealth is portrayed as leveling up in a video game. While it may be on-brand with Musk’s musing about the simulation hypothesis, it’s still a distracting choice that constantly calls attention to itself.

More successful is the trove of archival footage that Gibney pulls, beginning all the way back to Zip2 and PayPal, as well as Tesla. There, we see an awkward Musk in oversized dress shirts and a receding hairline before he gradually realized that he needed to look the part of an engineer. While Gibney is less interested in this early era of Musk—dedicating close to half of the entire runtime to Musk’s appalling time running DOGE and supporting right-wing causes under Trump 2.0—it’s nevertheless a fascinating portal into the person he would become. Told almost in its entirety by an interview with Justine Musk, Elon’s first wife, we can see the seeds of Musk’s disengagement with humanity and empathy, as well as the curdling of his relationship with fellow engineers and investors.

From there, Gibney quite rapidly moves through Tesla’s market dominance and woes, circling back to Musk’s claim of an autonomous self-driving car year after year until, eventually, he got something close to it, with the expected disastrous results. We hear from Martin Eberhard, Tesla’s co-founder that Musk eventually pushed out of the company. Yet it’s in the more recent, COVID-era Musk that Gibney seems particularly fascinated. As more than a few commentators suggest, COVID lockdowns triggered a type of break for Musk, who began obsessively pushing conspiracy theories on Twitter and traveling more right in his politics.

After a 10-minute intermission, the second half of Musk is when the horror movie truly begins, as it’s documented how he systematically started aligning himself with conservative figures and became more of a doomsday prepper, complete with an obsession about reproducing his genes. Here, Justine Musk is almost entirely supplanted by Ashley St. Clair, a former conservative influencer and mother of Musk’s son Romulus. St. Clair gives voice to the odd, nefarious ways that Musk exerts control over both his employees and the various mothers of his children through NDAs and monthly stipends. It’s a fascinating, shocking, nauseating dive into a world of legalese. When Trump gains back the White House in 2024, Gibney almost entirely abandons the weird salaciousness of Musk’s personal life to focus on DOGE and the absolute havoc that he and his tween employees wrecked on the federal government.

Of course, what lingers after the film are those who Gibney couldn’t interview. Grimes is oft-discussed but nevertheless a silent victim of Musk’s lack of empathy. His two-time ex-wife Talulah Riley is only given a passing mention. Outside a few former Twitter and U.S. Digital Service employees, we don’t have a full personal accounting of the devastation that his “takeovers” have wrought on those who were on the other end. Yet even with these absences, it nevertheless feels like Gibney has defined the man and distilled him to his basest form. Musk may not go down as the best documentary Alex Gibney has ever made, but it may be his most complete.
